resources.title: Choose a research method
resources.summary: Choose a method that can answer the decision, and check what the installed tools actually support.
steps: Name the decision, its owner, the relevant population and the uncertainty that matters. Review existing evidence before collecting more.

Use a prototype usability task to observe behavior. Use an implementation A/B/n comparison for differences between working designs on comparable tasks. The current A/B activity assigns one design per session; it is not a paired, within-person comparison.
Use a screenshot first-click test for the initial choice, not end-to-end task completion. Use preference comparisons for stated preference, not proof of better task performance.
Use card sorting to explore grouping and labels; use tree testing to assess findability in a text hierarchy. Neither alone establishes usability of the finished interface.
Use surveys for reported experience and interviews for explanations and context. Reported intention or confidence is not observed completion or comprehension.

Check the installed version before promising a workflow. Servant currently targets Studio 0.3.24 for draft imports; newer public releases may behave differently. The current runner does not provide participant recruitment, automatic clustering or a validated winning-design declaration.
Record alternatives and limits. Moderated sessions, interviews, field work and some accessibility questions need methods outside the unmoderated runner. Plan those with suitable tools and support.
questions: What evidence would change the decision?
Can this method measure the outcome, with this population and access needs?
Which work is supported here, and which needs another approved workflow?
resources.example: To learn whether people understand a waiting status, score their interpretation against a predefined rubric. A click, a preference or a claim of confidence alone does not establish that understanding.

resources.title: Plan a defensible study
resources.summary: Specify the question, task, scoring, recruitment, analysis and stopping rule before fielding.
steps: Cite prior research with its population, period, method and limits. Separate findings from hypotheses and business priorities; name the decision and its owner.

Define one primary outcome, the unit counted, numerator, denominator, scoring rule, treatment of missing outcomes and smallest difference worth acting on. Distinguish observed task success, self-report and tracking status.

For the current A/B/n activity, one session receives one design. Keep tasks and measurement comparable across designs. A paired study needs a separately suitable design, pairing and order controls; it is not a switch in this A/B activity.

Write a neutral participant task that does not reveal the intended answer. Write the accepted answer or success rubric separately for the scorer, including how partial or ambiguous answers are handled.

Define eligibility, recruitment, access needs, consent, device support and approved data handling before recruitment. Pilot with assistive technology when relevant; record remaining accessibility limits.

Justify the target using precision, power or a formative learning plan. Keep recruited, eligible, assigned, scored and follow-up-completed targets distinct. The comparison display minimum of 10 assigned per design is not a recommended sample size.

The standard A/B primary rate uses everyone assigned; dropout and unmeasured sessions remain in that denominator as not successful, with measurement status reported separately. Recruit extra for losses before assignment; later dropout is not removed from the assigned target. Do not forecast follow-up completion without a stated completion assumption.

Predefine primary contrasts, analysis, exclusions and a stopping rule. Record repeat-session risks: sessions are not verified unique people. Any recruitment controls belong in approved systems, not identifiers sent to an agent.

Pilot the exact versions, collection route, assignment, success signal and follow-up end to end. Recheck the plan after import into the installed Studio version. A generated draft or survey is not permission to field a study.
questions: Can another researcher score the primary outcome without guessing?
Are recruitment, assignment and follow-up targets using the correct units?
What must be checked or approved before real participants can enter?
resources.example: Participant task: You checked your refund status and see that processing is underway. What, if anything, would you do next? Keep the intended interpretation in a separate scorer rubric; do not put it in the participant prompt.

resources.title: Plan card sorts and tree tests
resources.summary: Use card sorting for grouping and tree testing for findability, with separate measures and limits.
steps: For a card sort, define the grouping question, audience, understandable card set and open, closed or hybrid format. Check that the set represents the content question without requiring unexplained specialist terms.

Preserve original participant labels only in the approved source system; document any normalization, merges and co-placement denominators in an approved analysis. Participant-written labels may contain private text. Servant deliberately omits open-sort participant group names from its saved readout; do not paste them into an agent to recover detail.

The current runner does not automatically produce clusters or dendrograms. If a separate approved analysis proposes a structure from co-placement, treat it as a hypothesis to test, not proven navigation.

For a tree test, version the text hierarchies, write realistic neutral scenarios and specify every acceptable destination and scoring rule before fielding. Do not repeat the destination label in the task.

Define destination success, direct success, first-branch correctness, backtracks and timing separately. Self-reported ease or completion is a different measure. State the denominator for each rate and the treatment of missing paths.

The current readout supports destination success, directness, first-branch correctness when known and backtracks. Lostness is not automatically calculated; any separate lostness analysis needs a stated definition and valid path data.

Account for multiple tasks from the same person and any paired comparisons; they are not independent participants. Plan the primary comparison and any multiplicity handling rather than choosing the best-looking task afterward.

Test the resulting interface for remaining usability and accessibility questions. A successful text-tree destination does not demonstrate that people can find or use the same feature in the visual interface.
questions: Am I asking about grouping, findability or the finished interface?
Does the task wording disclose the answer?
Are private participant labels and dependent observations handled correctly?
resources.example: Ask: You need to check what a letter sent last month asked you to do. Where would you look? Define the accepted destination in the scoring plan rather than naming that navigation item in the task.

resources.title: Run the study and record deviations
resources.summary: Check the whole collection route, preserve the declared denominator and document deviations.
steps: Pilot the exact version-pinned links, instructions, consent, assignment, keyboard flow and supported devices. Check comparable tasks and scoring for every design, including tracking unavailable and interrupted-session cases.

Use the field list generated for this study and its actual Qualtrics route. Do not invent fields or mix the two-survey link route with the embedded one-survey route. For the embedded route, do not also import a separate Survey 1.
Check that a success signal represents the intended behavior. A fired click event is not automatically comprehension or task success. Record self-report and tracker status separately.

Track recruited, eligible, assigned, task-scored and follow-up-completed counts separately. Runner counts are session-based; repeat sessions may be the same person. Check recruitment controls in the approved system without sending identifiers to an agent.

Keep the declared primary denominator. The standard A/B success rate includes everyone assigned: dropout and unmeasured sessions count as not successful. That is a rate convention, not proof of an observed task failure. Separately report missing measurement, dropout and measured-finisher rates; do not replace the primary rate with the most favorable one.

Investigate tracking differences, unequal dropout and version problems before interpreting a comparison. Preserve the original records in approved storage; log technical pauses, restarts, exclusions and protocol changes with their reasons and possible bias.
Follow the predefined stopping rule; do not stop because a preferred result appeared. Technical pauses are documented deviations, not a new opportunity to choose a favorable stopping point.

Keep raw Qualtrics/Medallia exports, participant labels, identifiers and session notes in approved systems. Use the existing approved local analysis workflow. Servant does not fetch survey responses; method-guide sync does not authorize transferring raw data to a model.
questions: Have both normal and broken collection paths been tested?
Are missing measurements distinguished from observed failures without changing the primary denominator?
What changed during fieldwork, and how could that affect the result?
resources.example: If B stops recording success signals, pause and investigate. Keep those assigned sessions in the predeclared primary rate as not successful; label their measurement status unknown or unavailable, not observed task failure. Report the defect and any resulting limits or exclusions transparently.
